title: What Managers Really Do All Day
text:
Classic management textbooks described the executive as a calm, reflective planner who spent the day organizing, coordinating and controlling. In the late 1960s the young Canadian researcher Henry Mintzberg decided to check by watching. For his doctoral work at MIT, he shadowed five chief executives, each for a full working week, and recorded every activity: every meeting, phone call, piece of mail and tour of the premises.

What he saw looked nothing like the textbooks. The executives worked at an unrelenting pace, with few breaks. Their days were broken into a large number of short episodes, and about half of their activities lasted less than nine minutes. They were constantly interrupted, and often seemed to welcome the interruptions. They strongly preferred talking, in person or by phone, to reading reports, and most of their time was spent in conversation with others. Truly reflective planning was rare.

From these observations Mintzberg described ten roles that managers play, grouped into interpersonal roles such as figurehead and leader, informational roles such as monitor and spokesperson, and decisional roles such as entrepreneur, disturbance handler and negotiator.
lesson: Leadership happens in fragments, conversations and interruptions. Accept that, but protect some time to think, or the urgent will crowd out the important.
location: Massachusetts Institute of Technology and five US organizations
source: Mintzberg, H. (1973). The Nature of Managerial Work. Harper and Row.
caveat: The core study observed only five executives, though later studies found broadly similar patterns.
